records.name: Ontario
records.current_summary: No province-specific anti-trans statute, policy or official hostility is on record: while two other provinces have legislated restrictions on trans names, pronouns or care, Ontario's government has not.  Criminal law and human-rights protection operate federally and uniformly. The national police-reported hate-crime series (Statistics Canada, March 2026) shows gender-identity/expression-motivated incidents rising nationally — +8% to 139 in 2024, a fourth consecutive increase — without identifying a trans-specific provincial pattern for Ontario.

sources.claim: Statistics Canada (30 Mar 2026, police-reported hate crime 2024): 4,882 hate crimes reported nationally (+1% on 2023), national rate 12.1 per 100,000. Ontario recorded the highest provincial rate at 16.0 incidents per 100,000 population, above the national figure — the only province-specific number in this release pointing above the national average. Federal criminal law and human-rights protections apply uniformly; police figures capture only reported incidents, and reporting is influenced by awareness and community trust.

CTV News reports (28 August 2023) that Ontario's education minister, Stephen Lecce, said parents 'must be fully involved and fully aware' of a child's decision to use a different name or pronouns at school, speaking the same week Saskatchewan joined New Brunswick in legislating parental consent for students under 16 who want to change names and pronouns; Lecce added that teachers and school boards already weigh 'exceptional circumstances' and potential harm to the child, and Ontario did not adopt such legislation at that time. The article documents the Ontario government's stance on pronoun and name rules in schools at the peak of the 2023 Canadian pronoun-policy wave - the province held the line against legislating parental consent.

The Ontario Human Rights Commission's policy on gender identity and gender expression states that under the Ontario Human Rights Code people are protected from discrimination and harassment on those grounds in employment, housing, facilities and services, contracts, and membership in unions, trade or professional associations; it defines gender identity as a person's internal and individual experience of gender, and notes that a chosen name and pronoun are common ways of expressing gender. The policy is the official provincial statement of the human-rights protections a trans person holds in Ontario's workplaces, housing and services.

The amendment sits in a government bill before the legislature, to be debated later in 2025, and is welcomed by Charlie Eau, executive director of Trans Manitoba. This documents Manitoba's official provincial position on trans people with dates, named officials and a local advocacy voice.

records.name: Yukon
records.current_summary: No territory-specific trans statute, incident series or policing pattern is on record for Yukon: the federal criminal law, the national gender-recognition framework and federal protections apply directly in this sparsely populated territory.  The national police-reported hate-crime series (Statistics Canada, March 2026) counts 139 gender-identity/expression-motivated incidents in 2024 — +8%, a fourth consecutive annual increase and nearly triple 2020 — and notes metropolitan areas report roughly 2.5 times smaller-town rates, so a territory without a metropolitan reporting hub carries thinner reporting infrastructure and thinner local data.

sources.claim: Statistics Canada release 'Police-reported hate crime in Canada, 2024' (published 30 March 2026): police reported 4,882 hate crimes in 2024 (+1% on 2023; +169% since 2018; rate 11.9 per 100,000). Hate crimes targeting gender identity or expression rose 8% to 139 — a fourth consecutive yearly increase and +184% since 2020; incidents targeting sexual orientation fell 26% to 658, though June (2024: 113 incidents) runs more than double the ~50-incident monthly average. Police-reported hate crime rates are ~2.5x higher in large metropolitan areas (13.9 per 100,000) than in smaller towns (5.5), which bears on sparsely-populated territories where reporting infrastructure is thinner.

Yukon News (31 March 2026) reports the Yukon Legislature marked International Transgender Day of Visibility on 30 March, with MLAs rising to speak: Yukon Party MLA Wade Istchenko (Kluane) praised 'the courage and resilience as well as the contributions and accomplishments of transgender, two-spirited, and gender-diverse Yukoners', acknowledged that 'too many people have experienced discrimination, harassment, and hate for far too long', and cited a national study showing transgender 15-17-year-olds face 7.6 times the risk of suicide attempt. The tribute is the territory's own cross-party, in-legislature acknowledgement of trans residents on record for Yukon.

Yukon News (29 April 2025) reports the Yukon government published community feedback on its LGBTQ2S+ Action Plan, the first of two check-ins the government committed to when the plan was released in 2021. Of 302 survey respondents, 267 were eligible (165 self-identified 2SLGBTQ community members, 102 allies); 65 per cent agreed banning conversion therapy was beneficial - over 70 per cent of 2SLGBTQ respondents and 55.9 per cent of allies - while 11.7 per cent of allies and 9.7 per cent of 2SLGBTQ respondents judged the ban not beneficial. The article confirms conversion therapy was banned in Yukon in 2020, a year before it became illegal nationwide - a dated, quantitative record of a territorial official plan and an existing territorial law.

Yukon News (13 June 2024) reports a Pride flag was allegedly vandalized and stolen from Holy Family Elementary School in Whitehorse's Porter Creek neighbourhood over a weekend in June 2024, and that a replacement flag was promptly put up. In a statement issued 12 June, Yukon Education Minister Jeanie McLean reaffirmed her commitment to the territory's sexual orientation and gender identity policy (SOGI 123), saying Pride month celebrates 'the diversity that makes the Yukon vibrant and strong'. This is the concrete Yukon incident on record - vandalism of a Pride symbol at a Whitehorse school - paired with an explicit territorial-government response.

records.name: England
records.current_summary: England is where the state's law applies without a devolved layer: there is no regional administration, and the national equality institutions and courts sit principally here. The decisive recent ruling for trans visitors is the state's Supreme Court decision of 16 April 2025 settling that ‘sex’ and ‘woman’ in the Equality Act 2010 mean biological or registered sex, and that an acquired gender certificate does not change legal sex for equality-law purposes. That definition is the ground on which services, searches and detention allocation operate for anyone detained here.  How detained trans people are allocated under that definition is being actively litigated: in a June 2026 ruling applying it, a court struck down prison guidance that had allowed identity-based placement, while in the same case the state's own lawyers argued a blanket birth-sex rule would breach human rights and pose unacceptable suicide risk. Allocation practice is therefore contested and risk-laden rather than settled.  No state-specific statute, ordinance or incident series survives in this record's sources; the audit found the earlier regional assertions (administrative facility codes, transport strip-search practice, recording gaps) uncited, so England is assessed on the imposed framework alone, with no documented local deviation in either direction.

sources.claim: BBC News (19 June 2026): a judge (Lady Ross, Court of Session) ruled Scottish Prison Service guidance allowing some trans prisoners to be housed by gender identity unlawful — sex segregation in prisons must be based on biological sex, applying the UK Supreme Court's April 2025 'definition of a woman' ruling. The judgment confirms the biological-sex custody logic that the same UK-wide ruling imposes on England's prison and custody decisions; the first minister said the government will consider the judgment (the Supreme Court had already held Article 8 confers no automatic right to opposite-biological-sex accommodation).

BBC News (5 February 2026): argument of the same judicial review, in which government lawyers said a blanket rule housing trans prisoners by sex at birth would breach human rights and create an unacceptable suicide risk, while For Women Scotland called the identity-based policy 'Orwellian'; the case tests how far the UK Supreme Court's April 2025 ruling (cited as the predicate for England's EHRC code and BTP strip-search policy) reaches into prison accommodation UK-wide.

The Home Office's England-and-Wales statistics (published 9 October 2025) record 115,990 police-recorded hate crimes in the year ending March 2025, with the transgender strand down 11% and the sexual-orientation strand down 2% against the previous year; the bulletin cautions that recorded figures understate prevalence - the Crime Survey estimate is about 176,000 hate-crime incidents a year - and that a February 2024 MPS recording-system change means earlier years over-counted. This gives the visitor the official England-and-Wales baseline for trans-hostile incidents in the jurisdiction where the national framework applies directly.

BBC News covers the UK Supreme Court's unanimous judgment in the For Women Scotland case (handed down 16 April 2025) that 'woman' and 'sex' in the Equality Act 2010 refer to biological woman and biological sex, meaning a gender recognition certificate does not entitle a trans woman to the Act's sex-based protections; Lord Hodge said the ruling should not be read as reducing the Act's protection against discrimination for transgender people. This is the grounding source for the record's core claim - the definition that governs services, searches and detention allocation in England.

BBC News reports (20 May 2025) that the Equality and Human Rights Commission - the body enforcing the Equality Act 2010 in England and Wales - updated its code of practice after the Supreme Court ruling, advising that services and businesses may ask for a person's birth certificate where there is 'genuine concern' about biological sex, and that trans people may be excluded from single-sex sport 'when necessary' for safety. This is the operative enforcement guidance a trans visitor to England meets at venues, transport and services day to day.

records.name: Queensland
records.current_summary: Queensland is assessed on the national framework. Same-sex conduct was decriminalised here in the 1990s reforms, and the current-status check found rights broadly advancing in line with the national standard since then.  The state's two earlier headline claims — a first-in-the-country criminal ban on conversion practices and a 2024 anti-discrimination rewrite modernising the gender-identity attribute — rest on sources that were unreachable at audit (a wire-service story behind a 401 wall; a state rights-commission page behind a 403), and one document previously cited for this region turned out to be another state's bill file. They are recorded here as unconfirmed rather than established. The state-level custody-placement divergence earlier attributed to Queensland likewise lost its citation.  What the audited record supports: no confirmed adverse state mechanism is on file either. A visitor should take the national baseline with lowered confidence in both the protective extras and any local hostility previously claimed for this state.

This confirms the record's first headline claim - Queensland was the first Australian state to enact a criminal ban on conversion practices - with a working source replacing the previously unreachable wire story.

This is a confirmed Queensland-specific adverse health-access measure in effect for the current visit window - the kind of local mechanism the audited record said was absent.

records.current_summary: Tasmania's record documented no state-specific statute, incident series or enforcement pattern beyond the national framework: decriminalised in 1997, with a 2021–22 reform arc that current-status research confirms left rights formally equal to everyone else's.  The one operational divergence earlier claimed for this state — prisoners placed on an explicit self-identification basis, shared with only a handful of the country's jurisdictions — lost its documentary support at audit: the file previously cited for it belongs to a different state, and the surviving sources for Tasmania were unreachable at fetch time (a 401-walled wire story and a 403-blocked commission page, both describing national developments). The custody claim is therefore treated as unconfirmed.

The article dates Tasmania's equality timeline precisely: after the Commonwealth Human Rights (Sexual Conduct) Act 1994 commenced on 19 December 1994, Tasmania still refused to repeal its anti-gay Criminal Code provisions and, faced with a likely High Court loss in Croome v Tasmania, decriminalised male homosexuality with effect from 14 May 1997 — the final Australian jurisdiction to do so. It records that the age of consent in Tasmania is 17 (one of only two jurisdictions with South Australia), that same-sex couples can enter into domestic registered partnerships in Tasmania with an optional official ceremony, that equality of adoption rights for same-sex couples applied in all states and territories from April 2018, and that as of 2019 Tasmania issues 'X' sex descriptors on birth certificates. Corroborates this record's account that Tasmania reached formal legal equality via the national framework with no state-specific incident series or enforcement pattern documented, while flagging the one standing statutory particularity — the 17 age of consent — not covered by the record's summary.

ABC News reported on 11 April 2019 that Tasmania's House of Assembly passed the Marriage Amendments Bill the previous day (10 April 2019) after Liberal Speaker Sue Hickey crossed the floor to vote with the Opposition, the legislation having already passed the Legislative Council. The reforms make gender on birth certificates optional, remove the requirement that transgender people undergo surgery for their gender to be recognised, and let people aged 16 or older change their registered gender without parental approval, with the Tasmanian Government having opposed the amendments and declining to rule out later repeal. State-specific enactment-level evidence for the equal-status finding in this record: the operational reform a trans visitor to Tasmania stands under, passed against government resistance rather than reflecting any criminalisation or incident series.

records.name: Roraima
records.current_summary: The national framework applies in Roraima with no documented state-level deviation: protections come from the federal supreme court — name and gender-marker change without surgery or court order, and the 2019 ruling equating anti-LGBT crimes with racism — rather than a comprehensive statute, and non-binary birth-certificate recognition is handled case-by-case state by state.  The country carries the world's highest absolute toll of killings of trans people, concentrated away from the capitals, and observers stress that protections are uneven in practice, thinning in the interior. The earlier specific claims for Roraima — no killings recorded for 2024, lowest national band for 2025 — lack a citation in this region's audited sources and are treated as unconfirmed; in so small a state a single case would dominate the statistics in any year, and official counts under-record.  For a visitor the picture is the national one with interior attenuation: rights on paper, thin services and enforcement, and no state-specific hostility mechanism on record either.

sources.claim: Country-framework page (revised through 2026): same-sex marriage legal nationwide via CNJ Resolution of 14 May 2013 (14-1 vote), adoption since 2010 (full rights 2015), and gender-marker change without surgery, hormones or diagnosis since the STF ruling of 1 March 2018. On 13 June 2019 the Supreme Federal Court held discrimination and violence on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity a crime equivalent to racism under Law 7.716/1989, punishable by imprisonment and fines. No third-gender option nationwide, but civil-registry 'non-binary/unspecified' entries have been possible since 2020 and a 6 May 2025 Superior Court of Justice ruling allows neutral-gender registry rectification as precedent. First transgender federal legislators (Salabert, Hilton) were elected in 2022.

OutRight International country report, last updated 12 March 2026: Brazil's LGBTIQ legal advances are significant but face repeal pressure in a conservative Congress. Brazil retains one of the world's highest rates of violence against sexual and gender minorities, particularly trans people. Gender-marker change proceeds by self-determination and trans voters may register under lived name and identity even before documents are updated. Over 3,000 openly LGBTQ candidates ran in the 2024 municipal elections, evidencing local political visibility.

Brazilian law-firm guide for expatriates (OAB/SP, updated April 2026): Brazil has among the most progressive LGBTQ+ protections in Latin America on paper - same-sex marriage (CNJ Resolution 175/2013), joint adoption, name and gender-marker change without surgery, and homophobia/transphobia criminalised as equivalent to racism (ADO 26 and MI 4733, 13 June 2019, imprisonment 1-5 years). Enforcement is uneven in practice: major cities (Sao Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, Brasilia, Belo Horizonte, Curitiba, Florianopolis) are broadly welcoming with established legal infrastructure, while smaller cities and rural areas may present more social friction despite identical legal rights.
